title: Sports
summary: The competition, community, and unforgettable stories that make every season feel different.

blocks.content:
## The game behind the game

I've followed sports closely since I was a kid, but what holds my attention now is less about the scoreboard and more about the decisions underneath it — roster construction, in-game adjustments, the relationship between analytics and instinct.

## Basketball

NBA is my main sport. I follow team-building strategy closely — how organizations think about draft capital, contract flexibility, two-way players, and building around a franchise anchor. The tension between conventional wisdom and data-driven scouting is something I find endlessly interesting.

## Football & Soccer

Football for the scheme complexity — how coordinators adapt across a season and how a single personnel package can break a defensive structure. Soccer for the tactical side: pressing systems, positional play, and how coaching identity shows up at the squad level.

title: History
summary: Looking backward to better understand how people, cultures, and ideas continue to shape the present.

blocks.content:
## Why history

I read history less for facts and more for the decision-making patterns inside it. The people who shaped events were usually operating under deep uncertainty, incomplete information, and the weight of precedent — conditions that feel familiar.

## What I find compelling

How institutions form around a crisis and then outlast their original purpose. How a single contingent event — a battle, a treaty, a miscommunication — sends a system down a completely different path. The gap between how decisions looked in the moment versus how they read a century later.

## Current interest

Late 19th and early 20th century — the period where modern organizations, states, and technologies were crystallizing simultaneously. The patterns from that era show up in how we think about institutions and coordination problems today.

title: Music
summary: The soundtrack to everyday life — a way to hold onto memories, moods, places, and people.

blocks.content:
## A soundtrack for everything

Music has a way of attaching itself to moments. A song can bring back a place, a person, or an entire season of life before I have time to think about why.

## How I listen

My listening changes with my surroundings — energetic when I need momentum, quieter when I want to think, and nostalgic more often than I expect. I enjoy finding new artists, but I always return to the songs that already feel like home.

title: Film
summary: Stories that make me laugh, sit with a new perspective, or keep thinking long after the credits.

blocks.content:
## Stories that stay with me

I love films that are entertaining in the moment and still leave something behind afterward — a question, an image, a conversation, or a perspective I had not considered before.

## What I notice

Character and atmosphere usually pull me in first. I enjoy seeing how writing, performance, sound, and visual choices work together to make a world feel honest, even when that world is completely unfamiliar.

title: Arts
summary: Finding new ways of seeing through design, photography, museums, and creative expression.

blocks.content:
## New ways of seeing

Art slows me down. Whether it is a photograph, an exhibition, an illustration, or a thoughtfully designed space, I enjoy noticing the choices that make something feel distinct.

## What I take with me

The arts remind me that there is rarely only one way to interpret an experience. They make me more attentive to detail, more comfortable with ambiguity, and more curious about how other people see the world.

title: Philosophy
summary: Making space for difficult questions about meaning, responsibility, and how to live thoughtfully.

blocks.content:
## Starting point

I came to philosophy through questions that kept resurfacing in other domains — what makes a decision rational, how to reason under uncertainty, when confidence is warranted versus when it's a failure of epistemic humility.

## Areas I read in

Epistemology — how we know what we know and what the limits of that are. Ethics — less the trolley problems and more the practical questions about responsibility, institutions, and how values interact when they conflict. Philosophy of mind, occasionally, when I'm in the mood to be confused.

## What I take from it

Mostly: intellectual honesty. Being willing to say "I don't know" or "I was wrong" is harder than it looks and worth practicing. Good philosophy teaches you to notice when you're sliding from reasoning to rationalizing.
